solution: Whether or not the demon lets a particle through, it returns to the centre wall every 2w/|vx| and its y-motion is an independent triangle wave of period 2h, so the set S_i of times at which particle i stands at (0,d) is fixed in advance and does not depend on any decision; each S_i is at most two arithmetic progressions found by solving the linear congruence 2w*vy*k = vx*(+-d - py) + vy*px (mod 2h|vx|) with the extended gcd, and its period is 4wh/g_i with g_i = gcd(2w|vy|, 2h|vx|). Every pass flips a particle's chamber, so only the parity of its passes matters: with eps_i = 1 iff particle i starts on the wrong side, the demon must choose a set D of trigger times such that the XOR over t in D of the bitmask chi(t) = {i : t in S_i} equals eps (all-or-none makes each time a single indivisible vector), and the answer is the least T such that eps lies in the GF(2) span of {chi(t) : t <= T}. Because all periods share the numerator 4wh, the whole event pattern repeats with period P = 4wh/gcd(g_i) <= 160000, so enumerating events in [0,P), grouping equal times, inserting each new bitmask into an xor-basis in time order and testing eps whenever the rank grows gives the earliest T, and eps never entering the span means impossible (a particle with vx = 0 on the wrong side is the simplest case). The event count is sum 2*g_i/gcd(g) which is at most about 1e7 (w=200, h=199, horizontal particles at y=d), each handled with a hash-dedup and a 200-bit reduction, so the whole thing runs in roughly O(E log E + (distinct vectors)*n^2/64), comfortably within limits in C++.
statement_summary: Two adjacent w-by-h chambers share a centre wall where a demon sits at height d. Up to 200 red or blue point particles with integer positions and velocities bounce elastically inside their chambers; whenever the demon chooses, every particle at its position crosses the wall, all or none. Find the earliest time when all red particles can be left and all blue right, or report impossibility.
notes: Verified three ways: both samples (24.0 / impossible); 4000 random small instances where the closed-form congruence solver agrees with an independent wall-by-wall event generator plus 2^n parity-state BFS (and a 3x longer horizon never turns an 'impossible' into a finite answer, confirming the period bound, while witness schedules are replayed physically); and 1391 instances (227 with a nontrivial answer) against a fully independent event-driven physics simulator that bounces each particle inside its actual chamber, branches reflect/pass at every (0,d) arrival and memoises exact configurations -- this checks the decision-independence claim itself, which is the crux. Confidence is 0.9 rather than higher only because the official time limit is unknown to me; the worst case is ~8e6-1.6e7 events (w=200,h=199, one particle with g=2 forcing P=79600 and the rest horizontal at y=d with |vx|=199), which needs C++ with 64-bit fraction comparison and vector dedup but no further idea. Deliberately NOT labelled: simulation (the whole point is that decisions need not be simulated; event times are closed-form), binary-search-answer (feasibility is not the interesting part; the span test is incremental), chinese-remainder-theorem (a single linear congruence per particle suffices), line-sweep/sorting (time ordering is scaffolding). 'geometry' covers the reflection-unfolding / triangle-wave argument; there is no canonical label for 'periodicity' or 'bouncing/reflection unfolding', which is the closest thing to a vocabulary gap here.
